title: Shia communities today
hookLine: in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, India and beyond

lines: A DISC OF CLAY ON THE MAT.
cards: A small disc of baked clay, about the size of a coin, sits on a prayer mat. When the person praying bows down, the forehead touches the clay.
You'll find discs like that in homes in Baghdad and Beirut, Baku and Manama, Karachi and Lucknow, Detroit and London. It's one quiet sign of a Shia household, among others.
The communities around it speak Arabic, Persian, Azerbaijani, Urdu, English. They live in Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, India and beyond. What holds them together?

teach.h: SHI'AT ALI: THE FOLLOWERS OF ALI.
teach.b: Shia is short for shi'at Ali, a phrase Shia Muslims explain as the followers of Ali.
Shia Muslims hold that after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, leadership belonged to his household, beginning with Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, and passing through a line of Imams.
They point, among other texts, to a hadith that Sunni collections keep too.
In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet says he is leaving two weighty things among his people: the Book of Allah, and his household, whom he asks them to remember. There are branches.
The Twelvers, named for the line of Imams they recognize, are one.
Zaydis, found especially in Yemen, and Isma'ilis, tomorrow's lesson, are others with their own histories. Then the places that hold a community.
In Iraq, Lebanon and Bahrain there is the husayniyya, a hall for gathering and mourning Husayn; in Pakistan and India the same kind of hall is called an imambargah.

There are seminaries in Najaf and Qom, where students train for years. And Twelvers follow a living senior scholar, a marja', on questions of law, so a believer in Chicago may follow a scholar in Najaf.

teach.h: THE SAME KA'BAH, THE SAME QUR'AN.
teach.b: Shia and Sunni Muslims pray toward the same Ka'bah, fast the same Ramadan, go on the same Hajj and read the same Qur'an.

Shia often join the noon prayer with the afternoon, and the sunset prayer with the night, and pray on that clay disc, which they explain as bowing onto earth, not onto a carpet. Different customs, the same direction.

how: Shia Muslims pray toward the Ka'bah like other Muslims, often joining the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers, and placing the forehead on a small clay tablet; they gather in mosques and in halls called husayniyyas or imambargahs, and Twelvers follow a living senior scholar, a marja', on questions of law.

o: Muslims who pray toward a different qibla
a single country's national form of Islam
Muslims who hold that leadership passed to Ali

games.q: you're a Twelver Shia Muslim in Chicago with a question of religious law. where do you turn?
o: to a marja', a living senior scholar, wherever he lives.
to whatever the majority of your neighbors do.
to no one: Shia law has no scholars.

practice: Choose one of the cities from the hook, Beirut, Baku, Manama, Lucknow, or a Shia center in your own city, and hold it in mind for a few breaths: people waking up there, praying there, going to work there.
If you pray, ask for good for them in your own words.
